extracted.intended_audience: historians of mathematics, classical scholars, editors and translators of ancient mathematical texts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and implicit standards for composing, editing, translating, and critically evaluating ancient Greek mathematical works (especially Euclid and related spherical geometry treatises). Useful for textual critics, translators, and historians reconstructing lost sources and assessing manuscript traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical structure of geometrical propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We have first the enunciation of the proposition in general terms, then the particular enunciation with reference to a figure with letters marking the various points in it, then the demonstration, and lastly, in some cases but not in all, the conclusion in terms similar to those of the enunciation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or editing Greek geometrical propositions, preserve the four-part classical form (general enunciation → particular enunciation with figure → demonstration → conclusion), while noting that the concluding formula may be absent in some cases. This form is evidence of the classical presentation already in use before Euclid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of unproved propositions as evidence of an earlier elementary textbook
rubrics_metrics.description: Autolycus (and Euclid) 'makes use of a number of propositions relating to the sphere without giving any proof of them or quoting any authority.' This indicates the prior existence of a text-book of the elementary geometry of the sphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reconstructing lost sources, treat the presence of unproved but used propositions as a signal that there existed an accepted elementary source; compare with later compilations (e.g., Theodosius's Sphaerica) where those propositions are proved to infer the content and order of the lost text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical ordering in spherical geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The geometry of the sphere at rest is of course prior to the consideration of the sphere in motion…’ Autolycus's On the moving Sphere assumes a prior treatment of the stationary sphere, its sections and properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating treatises on spherical geometry, place the study of the stationary sphere and its circles (great/small, parallels) before discussions of the sphere in motion (rotation, moving circles). This ordering reflects classical pedagogy and aids intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise technical definitions and adoption of technical shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid shortens 'the great circle defining the visible and the invisible portions of the sphere' into the technical term 'horizon' (opi?mv), and then defines it: 'Let the name horizon be given to the plane through us (as observers) passing through the universe and separating off the hemisphere which is visible above the earth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce technical terms with precise definitions and, where appropriate, adopt concise technical shorthand for repeated complex descriptions. Define new terminology explicitly the first time it appears to avoid ambiguity in later propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear operational definitions in observational/phenomenal astronomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Autolycus distinguishes 'true' and 'apparent' morning- and evening-risings and settings (e.g., 'true' morning-rising occurs at the moment of the sun's rising and is invisible; 'apparent' morning-rising is when the star is first seen before the sun).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For observational phenomena, give operational (observable vs. theoretical) definitions that separate ideal instants from visible appearances. Explicitly state observational criteria and the intervals during which objects are visible, as in the enunciations I.1, I.2, I.5, II.1, II.4, II.9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual-criticism principles for editing Euclid and related works
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars should prefer readings attested by the best manuscripts (e.g., Peyrard's MS 'P' and the best Theonine manuscripts), consult external ancient witnesses (Heron, Proclus, Sextus Empiricus), and be alert to interpolations (notably circa 3rd century); avoid extending Euclid's chains of propositions unjustifiably because predecessors used different lines of proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should (a) base editions on the most ancient and reliable witnesses (favor P where it preserves older readings), (b) use external sources such as Heron and Proclus to reconstruct earlier readings or detect interpolations, (c) note and justify any acceptance/rejection of alleged interpolations (e.g., extra axioms, additions to VI.33), and (d) avoid reconstructing long chains of dependencies from Euclid's arrangement when predecessors likely used different proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for identifying interpolations and original postulates/axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of manuscripts and ancient quotations shows that the Postulates were originally five, and many of the 'Common Notions' (axioms) in later manuscripts are interpolated; Heron and Proclus recognize only a subset of the axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing authenticity of definitions/postulates/axioms, cross-check with early commentators (Heron, Proclus) and ancient citations (e.g., Sextus Empiricus). Use internal consistency (positioning of Postulates as Postulates vs. Axioms) and external attestation to distinguish original from interpolated material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of a good mathematical translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ishaq's version 'seems to be a model of good translation; the technical terms are simply and consistently rendered, the definitions and enunciations differ only in isolated cases from the Greek, and the translator's object seems to have been only to get rid of difficulties and unevennesses in the Greek text while at the same time giving a faithful reproduction of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high-quality translation of mathematical texts should: render technical terms simply and consistently; preserve definitions and enunciations verbatim or with minimal deviation; clarify linguistic difficulties without altering mathematical content; and aim for fidelity to the original proofs and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for assessing independence and provenance of medieval translations/editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences such as the presence of Arabic words, arrangement differences (proofs preceding enunciations vs. usual order), word-for-word identity in definitions, and the inclusion/omission of books indicate whether a Latin edition was made from Arabic, from Greek, or is derivative/commentarial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish the source and independence of medieval translations, compare language traces (loanwords), ordering of material, identity of key passages (definitions/postulates), and manuscript evidence across versions (Athelhard, Gherard, Campanus, Commandinus). Use these markers to infer whether a translation is independent or dependent/commentarial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical and diagrammatic requirements for printed mathematical works
rubrics_metrics.description: The first printed edition (Ratdolt, 1482) required a method for producing figures; Ratdolt noted that difficulty of figures had hindered printing of mathematical books and that he discovered a method by which figures could be produced as easily as letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For printed dissemination of mathematical works, ensure that the printing technology or editorial method can reproducibly and clearly render geometric figures and diagrams; effective diagram production is essential for the usability and spread of a mathematical text.
